CC1.1-PF01: Leadership visibly backs ethical and security expectations through its own decisions and messaging, so staff see integrity treated as a priority rather than a slogan.
CC1.1-PF02: The organization has a written code of conduct that spells out expected behavior and is shared with staff and relevant outside parties.
CC1.1-PF03: Staff periodically acknowledge the code of conduct, and the organization checks whether people actually follow it through reviews, monitoring or reported issues.
CC1.1-PF04: Breaches of conduct are investigated and corrected promptly, with consistent consequences applied regardless of the person's role or seniority.
CC1.1-PF05: Contractors and vendor staff are held to the same ethical and conduct expectations as employees, typically through contracts, onboarding and acknowledgments.
CC1.2-PF01: The board or an equivalent governing body has defined, documented responsibilities for overseeing security, risk and internal control.
CC1.2-PF02: Board members collectively have the skills and experience needed to challenge management and oversee security and control matters effectively.
CC1.2-PF03: The oversight body includes members independent of management, giving it the objectivity to question decisions and hold executives accountable.
CC1.2-PF04: The board brings in outside advisors or specialists when it lacks in-house expertise on topics such as cybersecurity or privacy.
CC1.3-PF01: Management designs its organizational structure across all business units, subsidiaries, locations and outsourced functions so control responsibilities are covered everywhere.
CC1.3-PF02: Clear reporting lines exist so each role knows who it answers to and information on security and controls flows to the right decision makers.
CC1.3-PF03: Roles, approval authorities and responsibilities are documented and limited to what each position needs, supporting segregation of duties.
CC1.3-PF04: Security, compliance and other specialized responsibilities are explicitly assigned in job descriptions or charters, including any required by law or contract.
CC1.3-PF05: The organization defines who is responsible for managing vendors, customers and other external parties that affect its systems and controls.
CC1.3-PF06: A designated privacy function, such as a privacy officer, has clear authority and reporting lines to ensure legal and contractual privacy obligations are met.
CC1.4-PF01: Documented hiring, training and performance policies define the skills and competence expected for each role, especially those with security responsibilities.
CC1.4-PF02: Management regularly assesses whether staff and providers have the needed competence and takes action, such as training or reassignment, when gaps appear.
CC1.4-PF03: The organization recruits, mentors, trains and retains qualified people so it keeps enough capable staff to run its controls.
CC1.4-PF04: Succession and backup plans exist for key roles so critical security and control duties continue if someone leaves or is unavailable.
CC1.4-PF05: Background checks appropriate to the role's sensitivity are performed on new hires and contractors before they are given access.
CC1.4-PF06: Candidates' technical skills are verified against role requirements during hiring and when people move into technical or security positions.
CC1.4-PF07: Staff receive ongoing technical and security training, certifications or education so their skills stay current with technology and threats.
CC1.5-PF01: Management holds individuals accountable for their control responsibilities, with expectations tracked through the organizational structure and corrective action taken when needed.
CC1.5-PF02: Performance goals, incentives and rewards include security and control responsibilities, not just business results.
CC1.5-PF03: Management periodically reviews performance measures and incentives to confirm they still fit current objectives and don't encourage unwanted behavior.
CC1.5-PF04: Management watches for unrealistic targets or workload pressures that could push staff to bypass controls and adjusts goals or resources accordingly.
CC1.5-PF05: Individual performance reviews cover adherence to security and conduct expectations, leading to recognition or discipline as appropriate.
CC1.5-PF06: Staff who mishandle personal information or violate privacy policies face defined, consistently applied disciplinary consequences.
CC2.1-PF01: The organization defines what information it needs to operate and monitor its controls, and revisits those needs as objectives change.
CC2.1-PF02: Relevant data is collected from both internal sources, such as system logs, and external sources, such as threat intelligence and vendor reports.
CC2.1-PF03: Raw data is turned into usable information, such as reports, dashboards or alerts, that people can act on to run controls.
CC2.1-PF04: Controls keep data accurate, complete and protected as it is collected, processed and stored, so decisions rely on trustworthy information.
CC2.1-PF05: Data flow diagrams or similar documentation show how information moves through systems, interfaces and third parties.
CC2.1-PF06: A maintained inventory of hardware, software, data and other assets identifies each item and its owner.
CC2.1-PF07: Information is labeled by sensitivity, such as public, internal or confidential, so appropriate handling and protection rules apply.
CC2.1-PF08: Reports and data used to run or test controls are checked for completeness and accuracy before people rely on them.
CC2.1-PF09: The organization tracks where its assets and data physically and logically reside, including cloud regions and third-party locations.
CC2.2-PF01: Policies, procedures and control expectations are communicated to staff so everyone knows how to carry out their control responsibilities.
CC2.2-PF02: Management regularly reports to the board on security, risk and control matters so directors can exercise oversight.
CC2.2-PF03: Staff have an alternative, confidential channel, such as an ethics hotline, to raise concerns when normal reporting lines fail or are unsuitable.
CC2.2-PF04: Internal communications use methods suited to the audience and message, such as training, intranet posts, meetings or email, considering timing and sensitivity.
CC2.2-PF05: Employees and contractors are informed of their specific security and control duties through job descriptions, policies and onboarding.
CC2.2-PF06: Staff know how and where to report security incidents, system failures, policy violations and other concerns.
CC2.2-PF07: Business and security objectives, and any changes to them, are shared with staff who need them to do their jobs.
CC2.2-PF08: Regular security awareness training and communications keep staff informed about threats such as phishing and their part in preventing them.
CC2.2-PF09: Staff receive privacy training and communications explaining how to handle personal information and meet privacy obligations.
CC2.2-PF10: Personnel are told how to report suspected privacy incidents or breaches involving personal information, and to whom.
CC2.2-PF11: Internal staff have access to a description of how the system works, what it includes and where its boundaries lie.
CC2.2-PF12: The commitments and requirements the system must meet are communicated internally so staff understand what the system is designed to achieve.
CC2.2-PF13: Changes to the system that affect staff responsibilities or how work is done are communicated to them in a timely way.
CC2.3-PF01: The organization shares relevant control and security information with customers, vendors, regulators and other outside parties.
CC2.3-PF02: Customers, vendors and the public have open channels, such as support portals or contact addresses, to send concerns and information to the organization.
CC2.3-PF03: Relevant information from external parties, such as customer complaints or regulator findings, is passed on to the board.
CC2.3-PF04: External parties have a confidential or anonymous way, such as a whistleblower line, to report concerns outside normal contacts.
CC2.3-PF05: Communications to external parties use methods appropriate to the audience, sensitivity and legal requirements of the message.
CC2.3-PF06: Confidentiality commitments, and any changes to them, are communicated to customers, vendors and other parties who handle or rely on confidential data.
CC2.3-PF07: Privacy commitments, such as privacy notices and their updates, are communicated clearly to data subjects and relevant third parties.
CC2.3-PF08: Data subjects and external parties are told how to report privacy incidents, complaints or suspected misuse of personal information.
CC2.3-PF09: Customers and other external users receive a description of how the system works and what it does and does not cover.
CC2.3-PF10: Customers and relevant external parties are told what the system is designed to achieve and the service commitments it supports.
CC2.3-PF11: External users are informed of their own responsibilities, such as complementary user controls, for using the system securely.
CC2.3-PF12: Customers and other external users know how to report system outages, security incidents or other concerns, and how those reports are handled.
CC3.1-PF01: Leadership deliberately chooses its operational objectives, such as service levels and uptime targets, and documents how they tie to strategy.
CC3.1-PF02: Operational objectives state how much variation or underperformance leadership will accept, giving risk assessments a clear threshold to measure against.
CC3.1-PF03: Objectives cover both operational and financial performance targets, so risk assessments can show which risks threaten service delivery and which threaten results.
CC3.1-PF04: Documented objectives drive where budget, staff and technology are allocated, so investment decisions trace back to stated goals.
CC3.1-PF05: Financial reporting objectives are set to meet the accounting standards that apply to the organization, so reporting risks can be judged against them.
CC3.1-PF06: Financial reporting objectives account for what size of error or omission would matter to users of the reports, focusing risk work on significant items.
CC3.1-PF07: Financial reporting objectives are grounded in the organization's actual transactions and operations, so reports describe what really happens in the business.
CC3.1-PF08: Non-financial external reports, such as sustainability or security disclosures, are aligned to the recognized frameworks and standards the organization has adopted.
CC3.1-PF09: Objectives for non-financial external reports define how accurate and detailed the information must be for readers to rely on it.
CC3.1-PF10: Non-financial external reports reflect real events and activities across the organization rather than aspirational or selectively chosen information.
CC3.1-PF11: Leadership decides what internal reports it needs to run the business, and those choices shape the objectives for internal reporting.
CC3.1-PF12: Internal reports have defined accuracy and detail requirements so managers can rely on them when making decisions.
CC3.1-PF13: Internal reporting covers the organization's actual operations and events, giving management an accurate picture of what is happening.
CC3.1-PF14: Compliance objectives are built from the laws and regulations that apply to the organization, including aviation, privacy and security requirements.
CC3.1-PF15: Leadership defines how much compliance risk it will accept, generally with very little tolerance for breaking laws or regulations.
CC3.1-PF16: Top-level objectives are broken down into specific security, availability, confidentiality, processing integrity and privacy sub-objectives that risk assessments can target directly.
CC3.2-PF01: Risk identification covers the whole organization, including subsidiaries, divisions, business units and individual functions, not just headquarters or IT.
CC3.2-PF02: Risk assessments consider both internal factors, such as staffing and systems, and external ones, such as regulation, economic conditions and threat actors.
CC3.2-PF03: Managers at the right levels take part in identifying and analyzing risks, so those closest to each area contribute and own the results.
CC3.2-PF04: Identified risks are rated for likelihood and impact using a consistent method, so the organization knows which risks matter most.
CC3.2-PF05: Each significant risk has a documented decision to accept, avoid, reduce or transfer it, with an owner and planned actions.
CC3.2-PF06: The organization identifies threats, such as attackers, insiders, outages and natural events, that could stop it from meeting its system objectives.
CC3.2-PF07: Weaknesses in infrastructure, software, data, people and processes are identified, for example through vulnerability scans and architecture reviews.
CC3.2-PF08: Risk assessments cover threats and weaknesses introduced by vendors, partners and other third parties with access to systems or data.
CC3.2-PF09: Each risk's potential impact and likelihood are evaluated against objectives to decide which require treatment and how urgently.
CC3.3-PF01: Fraud risk assessments consider fraudulent reporting, theft or misuse of assets, corruption and unauthorized system access.
CC3.3-PF02: The organization examines pressures and incentives, such as aggressive targets or bonus structures, that could push people to commit fraud.
CC3.3-PF03: The organization identifies where weak controls, excessive access or poor oversight could give someone the chance to commit and conceal fraud.
CC3.3-PF04: Fraud assessments consider how individuals might justify misconduct, and whether the culture or past tolerance of wrongdoing makes this more likely.
CC3.3-PF05: Fraud risk analysis covers how IT systems and access to data could be abused, for example through privileged accounts, data changes or credential misuse.
CC3.4-PF01: The organization tracks external changes, such as new regulations, market shifts or geopolitical events, and assesses their effect on controls.
CC3.4-PF02: New products, services, locations, acquisitions or rapid growth trigger a review of whether existing controls still fit the business.
CC3.4-PF03: Changes in senior management or key personnel are reviewed for effects on control culture, oversight and knowledge of how controls operate.
CC3.4-PF04: New or significantly changed systems, platforms and technologies are assessed for new risks before and after they are introduced.
CC3.4-PF05: New, ended or changed vendor and partner relationships are evaluated for how they shift risk and affect controls.
CC3.4-PF06: The organization monitors the evolving threat landscape and newly discovered vulnerabilities, and updates its risk assessment when these change.
CC4.1-PF01: Monitoring combines continuous, built-in checks with periodic standalone reviews such as internal audits or independent assessments.
CC4.1-PF02: The frequency and depth of monitoring increase where the business, systems or risks are changing quickly.
CC4.1-PF03: Evaluations start from a documented understanding of how controls are designed and expected to work, so deviations can be recognized.
CC4.1-PF04: Control evaluations are performed by people who understand the controls, processes and systems being reviewed.
CC4.1-PF05: Ongoing monitoring is embedded in day-to-day operations, such as automated alerts and routine reconciliations, rather than being a separate exercise.
CC4.1-PF06: How often and how deeply controls are evaluated is adjusted according to risk, past findings and the significance of each control.
CC4.1-PF07: Periodic evaluations are carried out by reviewers independent of the control's operation, such as internal audit or external assessors, to ensure objectivity.
CC4.1-PF08: The organization uses varied evaluation methods, such as penetration tests, compliance audits, certifications and supplier reviews, to confirm controls are working.
CC4.2-PF01: Management or governance reviews the results of control evaluations to determine which issues are deficiencies and how serious they are.
CC4.2-PF02: Control deficiencies are reported promptly to the people responsible for fixing them and, when significant, to senior management and the board.
CC4.2-PF03: Corrective actions for deficiencies are tracked to completion, with owners, deadlines and verification that the fix actually works.
CC5.1-PF01: Control activities are mapped to the risks identified in the risk assessment, so each significant risk has controls designed to address it.
CC5.1-PF02: Control design takes into account the organization's size, environment, complexity, regulatory setting and operating model.
CC5.1-PF03: The organization identifies which business processes are relevant to its objectives and places controls within those processes.
CC5.1-PF04: The control set mixes preventive and detective, manual and automated controls so no single type carries all the risk.
CC5.1-PF05: Controls are applied at appropriate levels, from organization-wide policies down to individual transactions and system functions.
CC5.1-PF06: Incompatible duties, such as requesting, approving and executing changes, are split between different people, or compensating controls exist where separation is impractical.
CC5.2-PF01: The organization understands which business processes rely on technology and ensures general IT controls protect the systems those processes depend on.
CC5.2-PF02: Controls over networks, servers, databases and other infrastructure ensure systems are complete, accurate and available.
CC5.2-PF03: Security controls such as access management, authentication and monitoring protect systems and data from unauthorized access.
CC5.2-PF04: Controls govern how technology is acquired, developed, changed and maintained, including testing, approval and change management.
CC5.3-PF01: Documented policies and procedures turn leadership's directives into specific, day-to-day control activities that staff can follow.
CC5.3-PF02: Named roles are assigned ownership of carrying out each policy and procedure, and are held accountable for doing so.
CC5.3-PF03: Control activities are performed on schedule, so reviews, approvals and checks happen when they are supposed to, not after the fact.
CC5.3-PF04: Issues found while performing control activities are investigated and resolved, with follow-up action taken by those responsible.
CC5.3-PF05: Control activities are carried out by people with the skills, authority and training needed to perform them properly.
CC5.3-PF06: Policies and procedures are reviewed periodically and updated when the business, risks or technology change.
CC6.1-PF01: The organization keeps a current inventory of its systems, data stores and devices, each with an owner and classification, so access controls cover every asset.
CC6.1-PF02: New systems, cloud services and design changes are reviewed for access and security implications before they go live, not bolted on afterward.
CC6.1-PF03: Access to systems and data is limited to approved users and services through enforced controls such as role-based permissions and deny-by-default settings.
CC6.1-PF04: Every person and service is uniquely identified and must prove who they are, for example with passwords and MFA, before reaching protected resources.
CC6.1-PF05: Networks are divided into zones so sensitive systems are isolated from general traffic and a compromise in one area cannot spread freely.
CC6.1-PF06: Entry points such as VPNs, remote access gateways, APIs and admin consoles are known, limited in number and controlled.
CC6.1-PF07: Permissions on individual databases, files and applications are set so users reach only the information their job requires.
CC6.1-PF08: Rules for identity and login, such as password strength, MFA, lockout and session timeouts, are defined, applied consistently and kept up to date.
CC6.1-PF09: Service accounts, API keys, default passwords and other system credentials are inventoried, stored securely, rotated and never left at vendor defaults.
CC6.1-PF10: Sensitive data is encrypted at rest using approved algorithms wherever it is stored, including databases, backups and laptops.
CC6.1-PF11: Encryption keys are generated, stored, rotated and retired under controlled procedures, with access limited to a small set of authorized custodians.
CC6.1-PF12: Access to confidential business information is granted only to people who need it for an approved purpose, and its use is restricted to that purpose.
CC6.1-PF13: Personal data is accessible only to staff and systems that need it for the purposes disclosed to individuals, and is not used for anything else.
CC6.2-PF01: User accounts and credentials are issued only after a documented request is approved by the appropriate owner or manager.
CC6.2-PF02: Active accounts and credentials are reviewed periodically to confirm each one still belongs to a current, authorized user with a valid need.
CC6.2-PF03: Accounts and credentials are disabled promptly when someone leaves, changes roles or a contract ends, so stale logins cannot be used.
CC6.3-PF01: Granting or changing a user's access follows an approved request tied to their role, with records kept of who authorized it.
CC6.3-PF02: Access is revoked in a timely, tracked way when it is no longer needed, such as at termination, transfer or project completion.
CC6.3-PF03: Access is organized through defined roles or groups that enforce least privilege and keep conflicting duties separated.
CC6.3-PF04: Roles, group memberships and access rules are reviewed on a schedule by owners, and excess or conflicting permissions are corrected.
CC6.4-PF01: Badges, keys or entry rights to secure facilities are issued or changed only after documented approval based on job need.
CC6.4-PF02: Physical access rights are withdrawn promptly when people leave or no longer need entry, including deactivating badges and collecting keys.
CC6.4-PF03: Badges, keys, laptops and other company devices are collected back from departing staff and contractors.
CC6.4-PF04: Lists of who can enter secure areas, and entry logs, are reviewed periodically and unneeded access is removed.
CC6.5-PF01: Data and software are securely wiped or the media physically destroyed before equipment is discarded, resold or reused, with records of disposal kept.
CC6.6-PF01: Connections from outside the network are limited to approved sources, protocols and ports, with everything else blocked.
CC6.6-PF02: Passwords, tokens and other credentials used over external connections are protected from interception, for example through encryption and secure storage.
CC6.6-PF03: Remote and higher-risk access, such as VPN, admin or third-party logins, requires an extra factor or step beyond a password.
CC6.6-PF04: Firewalls, web gateways, intrusion prevention and similar tools guard the network perimeter and are configured and maintained to block threats.
CC6.7-PF01: Only authorized users and systems can send data out of the environment, with controls such as DLP or restricted file-sharing limiting transfers.
CC6.7-PF02: Data moving across networks is protected with encryption such as TLS or VPN tunnels, especially over public or untrusted links.
CC6.7-PF03: USB drives and other removable media are restricted, encrypted when allowed, and tracked to prevent data loss.
CC6.7-PF04: Laptops, phones and workstations are protected with measures like disk encryption, screen locks, device management and remote wipe.
CC6.8-PF01: Only authorized personnel can install or change software, with users blocked from adding unapproved applications.
CC6.8-PF02: Tools such as file integrity monitoring alert staff when software or configuration settings change without authorization.
CC6.8-PF03: Software and configuration changes go through a documented process of request, testing, approval and deployment.
CC6.8-PF04: Anti-malware or endpoint protection runs on servers and endpoints, stays updated and alerts on detected threats.
CC6.8-PF05: Files, email attachments and devices arriving from outside are scanned for malware or unapproved software before being allowed in.
CC7.1-PF01: Systems are built and maintained against documented hardening baselines, and deviations from those standards are identified and fixed.
CC7.1-PF02: Infrastructure and applications are continuously monitored for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations and signs of weakness.
CC7.1-PF03: Automated tools flag changes to critical files, settings or infrastructure so unexpected modifications are noticed and investigated.
CC7.1-PF04: The environment is regularly checked for unknown devices, software or cloud resources, and anything unauthorized is investigated and removed.
CC7.1-PF05: Internal and external vulnerability scans run on a regular schedule and after major changes, with findings tracked to remediation.
CC7.2-PF01: Documented monitoring procedures and tools, such as logging, SIEM and alerting, are in place to spot suspicious activity.
CC7.2-PF02: Monitoring is designed around known threats and critical assets so it catches unauthorized access, malware and unusual behavior.
CC7.2-PF03: Logs and events are filtered, correlated and analyzed to separate real anomalies from normal activity and noise.
CC7.2-PF04: Detection tools are checked regularly to confirm they are running, collecting data and generating alerts as intended.
CC7.3-PF01: Confirmed security incidents are handled through a defined response process with assigned owners and tracked actions.
CC7.3-PF02: Detected security events are reported to the right people and reviewed to decide whether they warrant incident handling.
CC7.3-PF03: Written procedures guide how staff investigate events to determine their cause, scope and severity.
CC7.3-PF04: When an incident occurs, the organization determines whether confidential business information was affected and how seriously.
CC7.3-PF05: Investigations establish exactly which confidential information was accessed, used or disclosed without authorization.
CC7.3-PF06: Incidents are evaluated to determine whether personal data was involved and what harm could result for the individuals concerned.
CC7.3-PF07: Investigations identify which personal data records and individuals were exposed, used or disclosed improperly.
CC7.4-PF01: Incident response roles, such as incident lead, technical responders and communications, are named and understood in advance.
CC7.4-PF02: Responders follow defined steps to contain an incident and limit its spread, such as isolating systems or disabling accounts.
CC7.4-PF03: Active incidents are mitigated in real time to reduce ongoing damage while the full response continues.
CC7.4-PF04: Incidents are worked through to closure, with the threat eliminated and resolution documented before the case is closed.
CC7.4-PF05: Affected systems and services are brought back into normal operation in a controlled way after containment.
CC7.4-PF06: A plan defines who is told about incidents, when and how, covering management, customers, regulators and other stakeholders.
CC7.4-PF07: Responders analyze what happened and how far it reaches before choosing a containment approach suited to the incident.
CC7.4-PF08: Weaknesses exploited or uncovered during an incident are fixed, for example through patching or configuration changes.
CC7.4-PF09: Progress and results of remediation work are shared with management and other affected parties.
CC7.4-PF10: After incidents, the organization reviews how well its response worked and updates the plan based on what it learned.
CC7.4-PF11: Incident records are reviewed periodically for trends and recurring issues that signal broader control weaknesses.
CC7.4-PF12: A defined breach procedure is followed when personal data is compromised, including legal and regulatory notification deadlines.
CC7.4-PF13: Individuals, regulators and other required parties are informed when personal data has been used or disclosed without authorization.
CC7.4-PF14: Staff or third parties who mishandle personal data face disciplinary or contractual consequences that are applied consistently.
CC7.5-PF01: Systems and data affected by an incident are restored from trusted sources, such as clean backups or rebuilt images, and verified.
CC7.5-PF02: Relevant details about the incident and recovery are shared with management, staff and affected external parties as appropriate.
CC7.5-PF03: Each significant incident is investigated to find its underlying cause, not just the immediate symptoms.
CC7.5-PF04: Control or system changes are made after an incident so the same problem is less likely to happen again and easier to detect.
CC7.5-PF05: Response and recovery procedures are updated with lessons learned from incidents and exercises.
CC7.5-PF06: Recovery plans are tested regularly through exercises or restore tests to confirm systems can actually be brought back.
CC8.1-PF01: Changes are governed by one consistent process from initial request through design, build, release and retirement of system components.
CC8.1-PF02: Each change request is reviewed and given permission to proceed by an appropriate owner before any work on it begins.
CC8.1-PF03: Changes are designed and built to agreed requirements and coding standards, in environments kept separate from live production systems.
CC8.1-PF04: Each change has a written record of what is changing, why, who is involved, and how it was built and verified.
CC8.1-PF05: A ticketing or change log tracks every system change and its current status so nothing reaches production untracked.
CC8.1-PF06: Software and system settings are configured to approved, hardened standards, and configuration changes follow the same controlled process.
CC8.1-PF07: Changes are tested in a non-production environment, with results recorded, before they are allowed into the live system.
CC8.1-PF08: A designated authority reviews test results and signs off on each change before it is released to production.
CC8.1-PF09: Approved changes are released to production in a controlled way, with rollback plans and checks that deployment succeeded.
CC8.1-PF10: The organization identifies needed changes and evaluates their security, operational and business impact before deciding whether to proceed.
CC8.1-PF11: Lessons from security incidents feed into the change process, so fixes to systems, data, software or procedures are identified and made.
CC8.1-PF12: Documented standard configurations exist for servers, network devices and endpoints, and systems are compared against them to spot drift.
CC8.1-PF13: A defined fast-track path lets urgent fixes go in quickly, with authorization and documentation completed afterward.
CC8.1-PF14: Security patches and updates are identified, prioritized, tested and applied within set timeframes through the change process.
CC8.1-PF15: Changes are assessed for their effect on uptime and recovery, so updates do not weaken redundancy or availability of the system.
CC8.1-PF16: Change work keeps confidential data protected, for example by keeping real sensitive data out of test environments or masking it.
CC8.1-PF17: Changes are reviewed so personal information stays protected, such as avoiding live personal data in development and testing.
CC8.1-PF18: Privacy requirements are built into new systems and changes from the start, limiting personal data collection and exposure by default.
CC9.1-PF01: The organization plans for disruptive events and puts measures such as continuity and recovery arrangements in place to limit business impact.
CC9.1-PF02: Leadership evaluates whether insurance, such as cyber or business interruption cover, should absorb part of the financial loss from major incidents.
CC9.2-PF01: Security, service and compliance expectations for vendors and partners are defined up front and written into contracts or agreements.
CC9.2-PF02: The organization identifies weaknesses that vendors and partners could introduce, such as insecure connections, products or access to its data.
CC9.2-PF03: Vendors and partners are risk-assessed before onboarding and periodically after, scaled to their access to systems and data.
CC9.2-PF04: Named owners are responsible for each vendor or partner relationship, including oversight of security, performance and contract obligations.
CC9.2-PF05: Agreed channels and contacts exist for exchanging information with vendors and partners, including how security incidents get reported both ways.
CC9.2-PF06: There is a defined process for handling vendor or partner shortfalls, deviations from agreed terms, or requests for exceptions.
CC9.2-PF07: Vendor and partner performance against service levels and security obligations is reviewed regularly, using reports, audits or attestations.
CC9.2-PF08: Issues found during vendor reviews are recorded, followed up with the vendor, and tracked until fixed or formally accepted.
CC9.2-PF09: Ending a vendor relationship follows a defined process covering revoking access, returning or destroying data, and transitioning services.
CC9.2-PF10: Vendors and partners who handle confidential information sign agreements binding them to protect it and limit its use and disclosure.
CC9.2-PF11: The organization checks that vendors and partners actually honor their confidentiality obligations, through reviews, attestations or audits.
CC9.2-PF12: Vendors and partners that process personal information commit in writing to privacy obligations consistent with the organization's own commitments.
CC9.2-PF13: The organization verifies that vendors and partners handle personal information as their privacy commitments require, and acts on gaps.
A1.1-PF01: System capacity such as compute, storage and network usage is monitored continuously against defined thresholds to keep services available.
A1.1-PF02: Future capacity needs are projected from usage trends and planned business growth so shortfalls are anticipated before they affect availability.
A1.1-PF03: Capacity forecasts lead to concrete actions, such as adding resources or rebalancing workloads, before demand outstrips supply.
A1.2-PF01: Environmental risks to facilities and equipment, such as fire, flood, power loss and overheating, are identified and assessed.
A1.2-PF02: Facilities have measures in place to detect environmental problems, such as smoke, water, temperature and humidity sensors.
A1.2-PF03: Protective equipment such as fire suppression, UPS, generators and cooling is installed, serviced and kept in working order.
A1.2-PF04: Environmental monitoring raises alerts on abnormal conditions so staff can investigate and act before systems are affected.
A1.2-PF05: Documented procedures guide staff in responding to environmental events to protect equipment and restore normal operations.
A1.2-PF06: Environmental incidents are reported to the right people and reviewed afterward to improve protections and response.
A1.2-PF07: The organization identifies which systems and data must be backed up, and how often, based on business and recovery needs.
A1.2-PF08: Backups run on a defined schedule, are monitored for success, and failures are investigated and corrected.
A1.2-PF09: Backup copies are kept at a separate, protected location, physical or cloud, so a single site loss cannot destroy them.
A1.2-PF10: Secondary or redundant infrastructure is available so critical processing can continue or resume if the primary environment fails.
A1.2-PF11: Recovery objectives are defined and backup and replication approaches are chosen so data can be restored within acceptable loss limits.
A1.3-PF01: The business continuity and disaster recovery plans are exercised regularly, with results reviewed and the plans updated accordingly.
A1.3-PF02: Restores from backup are tested periodically to confirm the data comes back complete, uncorrupted and usable.
C1.1-PF01: The organization defines what counts as confidential information and identifies and labels it as it is created or received.
C1.1-PF02: Confidential information is kept only for the period required by commitments, contracts or law, under a defined retention schedule.
C1.1-PF03: Confidential information is safeguarded against accidental or unauthorized deletion or loss while it must still be retained.
C1.2-PF01: Confidential information that has reached the end of its retention period is identified and flagged for disposal on a regular basis.
C1.2-PF02: Confidential information is disposed of securely, using methods such as wiping, shredding or crypto-erasure, with records of destruction kept.
PI1.1-PF01: The organization documents what the system must do and how it must perform, including the data it needs to process correctly.
PI1.1-PF02: The data required to deliver each product or service, including its sources, format and quality, is defined and documented.
PI1.1-PF03: Users are given the information they need to use the product or service correctly, such as specifications, instructions and limitations.
PI1.2-PF01: Required characteristics of incoming data, such as format, completeness, valid ranges and sources, are defined for each input.
PI1.2-PF02: Inputs are validated against defined rules when received, and errors or rejected items are flagged and corrected.
PI1.2-PF03: Records of data entering the system are kept, showing what was received, when and from where, to support reconciliation.
PI1.3-PF01: The organization documents how data must be processed, including the rules, calculations and expected outputs for each function.
PI1.3-PF02: The processing steps, schedules and responsibilities for each system activity are defined so work runs consistently.
PI1.3-PF03: Processing errors and failed jobs are detected through checks and monitoring, then investigated and corrected in a timely manner.
PI1.3-PF04: System processing activity is logged so what ran, when and with what result can be traced and reviewed.
PI1.3-PF05: Inputs are processed completely, accurately and on time according to the defined specifications.
PI1.4-PF01: System outputs such as reports and files are protected from unauthorized access, change or loss.
PI1.4-PF02: Outputs are delivered only to authorized recipients, with controls that confirm the correct destination before release.
PI1.4-PF03: Checks such as reconciliations and control totals confirm that outputs are delivered in full and without errors.
PI1.4-PF04: Records of output generation and distribution are kept, showing what was sent, to whom and when.
PI1.5-PF01: Data and items held in storage are protected from unauthorized access, change, theft or damage.
PI1.5-PF02: System records are archived on a defined basis and protected so they remain intact and retrievable when needed.
PI1.5-PF03: Stored data is checked to remain complete and accurate, with integrity controls that catch corruption or unintended changes.
PI1.5-PF04: Records of storage activities, such as data being written, changed, moved or deleted, are kept and available for review.
P1.1-PF01: The organization tells individuals what personal information it handles, why, and how they can reach it with privacy questions or concerns.
P1.1-PF02: Individuals receive a privacy notice at or before the point their personal information is collected, or as soon as practical afterward.
P1.1-PF03: The privacy notice names which business units, affiliates, websites, and processing activities it applies to, so nothing in scope is left unexplained.
P1.1-PF04: Privacy notices are written in plain wording, kept up to date, and posted where individuals can easily find them, such as a website footer or signup page.
P1.1-PF05: The organization reviews its privacy notice on a set schedule and whenever practices change, confirming it still matches how data is actually handled.
P1.1-PF06: When the privacy notice changes, the organization alerts affected individuals in advance or promptly, explaining what changed and how it affects them.
P1.1-PF07: Earlier versions of the privacy notice are archived with their effective dates, so the organization can show which terms applied at any point.
P2.1-PF01: Individuals are told what choices they have about how their personal information is collected, used, shared, and kept, and how to exercise them.
P2.1-PF02: Individuals learn what happens if they refuse or later withdraw consent, such as losing access to certain services or features.
P2.1-PF03: The organization captures consent before relying on personal information, using opt-in or opt-out mechanisms appropriate to the data and applicable law.
P2.1-PF04: Before reusing personal information for a purpose not originally disclosed, the organization records the new use and gets fresh consent where required.
P2.1-PF05: Sensitive data such as health, biometric, or financial details is only collected or used after individuals give clear, affirmative, documented consent.
P2.1-PF06: Individuals agree before their personal information is transferred to other parties or across borders, and that consent is recorded.
P3.1-PF01: The organization collects only the personal information needed for its stated purposes, and data-gathering forms and systems avoid asking for extras.
P3.1-PF02: Personal information is gathered honestly and legally, without deception, hidden tracking, or coercion, and collection methods are reviewed for compliance.
P3.1-PF03: Personal information obtained from third parties or public sources comes from vetted, trustworthy providers whose data practices are lawful and accurate.
P3.1-PF04: When the organization obtains extra information about individuals from other sources, it tells them what was acquired and why.
P3.2-PF01: Before asking for explicit consent, individuals are told what will happen if they decline, such as a service they cannot receive.
P3.2-PF02: Explicit consent is captured in a retrievable record showing who agreed, when, and to what, and that record is kept for evidence.
P4.1-PF01: Personal information is used only for the purposes disclosed to individuals, with access controls and reviews that stop unrelated or secondary use.
P4.2-PF01: A retention schedule defines how long each type of personal information is kept, and records are held no longer than needed or legally required.
P4.2-PF02: Personal information kept under retention rules stays protected against loss, alteration, or unauthorized access for as long as it is stored.
P4.3-PF01: The organization logs and tracks individuals' deletion requests and marks the affected records so they are reliably removed or excluded from use.
P4.3-PF02: Personal information that is no longer needed is disposed of, anonymized, or redacted using approved methods, and disposal is documented.
P4.3-PF03: Personal information on paper, devices, and backups is irrecoverably destroyed through shredding, secure wiping, or certified destruction once its retention ends.
P5.1-PF01: As a processor, the organization helps its client controllers fulfill individuals' access requests promptly and within agreed timeframes.
P5.1-PF02: Before releasing personal information, the organization verifies the requester's identity so data is never disclosed to an impostor.
P5.1-PF03: Individuals can request and view the personal information held about them through a defined, accessible process such as a portal or request form.
P5.1-PF04: Personal information is returned to requesters in a readable, plain format and within a reasonable or legally set response period.
P5.1-PF05: When an access request is refused, the individual is told in writing, with the reason and any options to challenge the decision.
P5.2-PF01: As a processor, the organization acts on controllers' instructions to correct or update personal information and confirms when changes are made.
P5.2-PF02: Individuals whose access requests are refused receive a written explanation of the reason, as permitted by law, and how to dispute it.
P5.2-PF03: Individuals can ask to fix or update inaccurate personal information, and the corrections are applied and passed to others who received the data.
P5.2-PF04: When a correction request is declined, the individual is told why and can have their disagreement noted alongside the record.
P6.1-PF01: Third parties receiving personal information are informed of the organization's privacy requirements, typically through contracts or data-processing agreements.
P6.1-PF02: Personal information is shared only for disclosed purposes, with consent where required, or when the law compels it, and each release is checked first.
P6.1-PF03: Personal information goes only to vetted recipients who need it and are bound to protect it, rather than to any party that asks.
P6.1-PF04: Before sharing personal information with third parties for a new purpose, the organization informs individuals and obtains consent where required.
P6.2-PF01: The organization keeps a complete log of each approved release of personal information, recording what was shared, with whom, when, and why.
P6.3-PF01: Every detected or reported unauthorized disclosure of personal information is logged with details of what happened, the data involved, and the response.
P6.4-PF01: The organization periodically checks, through audits, questionnaires, or reports, that vendors handling personal information keep their contractual privacy commitments.
P6.4-PF02: When a vendor misuses personal information, the organization takes corrective action such as requiring fixes, restricting access, or ending the relationship.
P6.4-PF03: Vendor agreements require third parties to promptly notify the organization of any unauthorized disclosure of personal information they detect.
P6.5-PF01: When a vendor reports or is found misusing personal information, the organization investigates and drives corrective actions to contain and fix the problem.
P6.5-PF02: Vendors notify the organization quickly of actual or suspected unauthorized disclosures, and those notices trigger the incident response process.
P6.6-PF01: The organization maintains a current list of breach notification obligations by jurisdiction and contract, including who must be told and the deadlines.
P6.6-PF02: After a breach involving personal information, affected individuals, regulators, and other required parties are notified accurately and within mandated timeframes.
P6.7-PF01: As a processor, the organization supplies controllers with the disclosure details they need to answer individuals' requests for an accounting of disclosures.
P6.7-PF02: The organization knows which types of personal information it holds and how each is handled, so it can accurately report what was disclosed.
P6.7-PF03: Requests for an accounting of disclosures are logged, routed to the right team, and answered with a clear list of who received the individual's data.
P7.1-PF01: Personal information is validated at entry and periodically reviewed so records remain correct, complete, and up to date for their intended use.
P7.1-PF02: The organization periodically confirms that the personal information it holds is still relevant to its stated purposes and removes data that is not.
P8.1-PF01: Individuals and client controllers are told how to submit privacy questions, complaints, or disputes and whom to contact.
P8.1-PF02: Privacy inquiries, complaints, and disputes are logged, investigated, and resolved within defined timeframes, with outcomes communicated back to the requester.
P8.1-PF03: The dispute-resolution process and available recourse, such as independent arbitration or regulator escalation, are documented and shared with individuals.
P8.1-PF04: Results of privacy compliance reviews are documented and reported to management, with corrective actions tracked to closure.
P8.1-PF05: Instances of privacy noncompliance are recorded, reported to the appropriate leaders, and tracked until they are resolved.
P8.1-PF06: The organization continuously monitors privacy controls and practices, using reviews, metrics, or audits to catch noncompliance early.
